claims.text: Circuits returned under specifications that differ only in defensible analytic choices are almost disjoint in their edges. Structural overlap must be read against chance, and it is not the quantity a filing depends on.
methods: Pre-registered crossed multiverse grid over seven analytic axes, every level taken from a published implementation
Structural comparison of edge sets in GPT-2 small's factorised graph (tens of thousands of edges)
results: Random subsets of a few hundred edges are expected to share almost nothing, so beating chance overlap is a weak bar
conditions: Structural difference need not imply functional or statement difference

claims.text: When circuits are mapped through a fixed deterministic claim map to Annex IV / Article 86-style statements, the claim flips on about three quarters of specification pairs. The flips include substantive disagreement about which region of the network is responsible, even at the coarsest granularity.
methods: Deterministic claim map from circuit to natural-language statement, not a language model
Two addressees: the overseer (where the behaviour is carried and how concentrated it is) and the affected person (which input parts drove the decision)
Nested granularities
Specification curve presentation
results: Claim flips on three quarters of pairs (Section 7.2)
conditions: The claim map is fixed in advance
Discretisations such as size categories come from a committed calibration rule

claims.text: No single analytic axis rescues the filing. Holding any one axis fixed does not remove the disagreement, and the axes that govern structure need not be those that govern statements.
methods: Holding each axis fixed in turn and comparing within its levels
results: No analytic axis rescues the filing (Section 7.3)
Standardising the metric would still leave six axes free
conditions: Standardisation decisions should be made at the level of the statement

claims.text: Disagreement persists under maximum pressure. With size-dependent content removed from the statement and only same-size circuits compared, attribution of the behaviour to a region still varies.
methods: Size-matched comparison with the statement reduced to region attribution, the core of an Annex IV 2(b) account
results: The result holds under maximum pressure (Section 7.4), so the disagreement cannot be attributed to the size channel
conditions: Circuit size is an outcome chosen by the threshold rule, not an axis

claims.text: Pooled comparisons against a size-matched random baseline mislead, so within-size comparison is required. Circuit size is a hidden channel in multiverse designs.
methods: Random edge subsets of matched size passed through the same claim map
Within-size decomposition
results: At large sizes a uniform random draw touches every component and can support only one statement
A pooled direction can point either way for reasons unrelated to discovery quality
conditions: A pooled baseline result reported without its within-size counterpart is uninterpretable

claims.text: Over part of the size range, filings differ more than mechanisms do. This is assessed by chance-corrected, example-level functional agreement, which addresses the phantom specialisation objection.
methods: Example-by-example success/failure agreement using the measures of Bayat Makou et al.
Cohen's kappa to correct for agreement expected from accuracy alone
results: Statement disagreement exceeds functional disagreement over part of the range (Section 7.6)
conditions: Where mechanisms differ more than statements, the procedure is coarser than the mechanisms; where statements differ more, it amplifies differences

claims.text: A five-item filability disclosure protocol is implementable without the regulator adjudicating which analytic choice is correct.
methods: Declare the specification space with citations
Publish the claim map as deterministic code
State the chosen specification and why it was selected
Report discard rates per axis level
Report pooled statistics with their within-group (within-size) decomposition
results: Cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit
conditions: Covers what a careful paper should already report

claims.text: The design is pre-registered and bounded by the library. Its conclusions are conservative relative to the literature and are limited to one model and one task.
methods: Grid of 7 objectives x 7 operators x 4 corruptions nested in 5 operators x 4 metrics x 3 thresholds x 2 prompt variants x 5 seeds = 1,540 discovery cells and 18,480 specifications
Discards recorded, not repaired
Bootstrap over specifications, not pairs
Pre-registered Pythia-160m replication of 924 cells with 3 seeds
results: Optimal ablation is not in the library and is therefore excluded
343 tests; numeric tokens verified against stored outputs
conditions: The seed selects sampled prompts and so measures evaluation-set variability, not nondeterminism
Bootstrap is unreliable for small groups
A second task is designed but not run

items.question: Why does the grid contain 1,540 discovery cells but 18,480 specifications?
items.answer: The metric (4 levels) and threshold (3 levels) are applied to a circuit after discovery rather than changing the discovery run. Each discovery cell (objective x operator/corruption combination x prompt x seed = 7 x 22 x 2 x 5) therefore yields 4 x 3 = 12 specifications.
rubric: States that each discovery cell yields 12 specifications (18,480 = 1,540 x 12)
Attributes the factor of 12 to the 4 metrics x 3 thresholds applied after discovery

items.question: Why does the pre-registered Pythia-160m replication have 924 cells?
items.answer: The objective x operator/corruption combinations give 7 x (2 + 5 x 4) = 154, and the 2 prompt variants double this to 308. With only 3 seeds instead of 5, that gives 924 discovery cells, i.e. 1,540 x 3/5.
rubric: Identifies the seed axis reduction from 5 to 3 as the only difference
Shows the arithmetic: 154 x 2 x 3 = 924, or equivalently 1,540 x 3/5

items.question: Suppose discovered circuits in some part of the grid are mostly large. Why could a pooled random-baseline comparison make them look less statement-stable than random subgraphs, even if discovery is sound?
items.answer: At large sizes a random draw touches every component and can support only one statement, so random pairs agree perfectly there while discovered circuits can still vary. Pooling across sizes then favours the random baseline for reasons unrelated to discovery quality.
rubric: Says random large draws all yield the same single statement, so their agreement is trivially high
Says the pooled comparison mixes size distributions, so the apparent inferiority reflects size rather than discovery quality

items.question: Why does drawing every level from the Miller et al. library make the paper's instability findings hard to dismiss as the product of unreasonable settings?
items.answer: Every level is one the tool's own authors expose as a usable configuration, and none was invented for the study. A critic therefore cannot say the varied choices are indefensible without criticising the tooling's own definitions.
rubric: States that the levels are published or exposed by the tool itself rather than invented
Concludes that any disagreement arises among choices that count as defensible by the tooling's own standards

items.question: Why would repairing cells that fail to execute undermine the study, given what the study is testing?
items.answer: The library is the instrument under test, so repairs would alter the instrument and introduce post-hoc analytic choices. That is exactly the undisclosed flexibility the paper is warning about. Recording discards with their rates keeps the evidence's composition visible instead.
rubric: Notes that repairing changes the instrument under test
Notes that post-hoc repair is itself analytic flexibility that could shape results, so discards should be recorded and reported instead

items.question: Why is the flip in which region is held responsible problematic for the Article 86 addressee, and not only for the overseer?
items.answer: The coarsest statement available rests on undisclosed choices, and finer statements refine the coarse one rather than replacing it. A flip at the region level therefore propagates to every granularity, including the one offered to an affected person.
rubric: States that the disagreement occurs even at the coarsest granularity
Explains that nested, finer statements refine the coarse one, so no addressee's account escapes the flip

items.question: Within-axis conditioning groups in the Pythia-160m replication will be smaller than in the GPT-2 grid. Would bootstrap intervals for those within-group quantities be more or less trustworthy, and what should be reported instead?
items.answer: They would be less trustworthy. With 3 seeds instead of 5, each conditioning group holds fewer specifications, and the paper says bootstrap fails for small groups. Point estimates with diagnostics should be reported instead.
rubric: Says less trustworthy
Links this to fewer specifications per group (3 seeds vs 5) and the paper's small-group bootstrap limitation
Recommends point estimates with diagnostics

items.question: If the claim map had used a language model to write statements, could the three-quarters claim-flip rate still be read as evidence about circuit variation? Why?
items.answer: No. Model variance in statement generation would add to circuit variance, with no way to separate the two, so the flip rate could partly reflect the language model rather than the circuits.
rubric: Says no, the flip rate would no longer be attributable to circuits
Explains that language-model variance confounds circuit variance and cannot be separated from it

items.question: Suppose the threshold rule gave every metric's circuits a distinct, non-overlapping size band. What could the size-matched control in Section 7.4 then fail to test?
items.answer: Same-size pairs would only ever share a metric, so the control could not test whether changing the metric flips region attribution. Metric effects would be confounded with size and left unexamined.
rubric: Says cross-metric disagreement would go untested under the size-matched control
Explains that size-matched pairs would all share a metric because size is an outcome tied to the metric

items.question: Two circuits each succeed on nearly every IOI prompt and agree on most examples. Would that raw agreement show that they implement the same mechanism?
items.answer: No. With both near-perfect accuracy, high agreement is expected by chance alone. Only chance-corrected agreement such as Cohen's kappa can separate the same mechanism from mere similar accuracy.
rubric: Says no
Explains that high accuracy produces high raw agreement by chance, so a chance-corrected measure such as kappa is needed

items.question: If the metric-relative threshold rule discarded most specifications under one metric, would the pooled claim-flip rate still describe the balanced design? Why?
items.answer: No. The surviving pool would under-represent that metric, so the pooled rate would mainly reflect the other metrics. This is why discard rates per axis level must be reported.
rubric: Says no
Explains that the surviving pool's composition departs from the balanced grid, so per-level discard rates must be reported

items.question: In the large-size region, discovered circuits show lower statement agreement than random subsets. Would that imply discovery performs worse than random there?
items.answer: No. The random baseline is degenerate there: every draw touches every component and supports the same one statement. The baseline's perfect agreement says nothing about discovery quality.
rubric: Says no
Explains that the baseline is degenerate at large sizes, supporting only one statement

items.question: If discovered circuits shared clearly more edges than chance, would that establish that their filed statements are compatible?
items.answer: No. Exceeding chance overlap is a weak bar in a graph this large. Circuits with considerable overlap may still support different statements, because filings depend on statements, not edges.
rubric: Says no
Cites both reasons: beating chance is a weak bar, and structural overlap is not the quantity the statement depends on

items.question: Would adding a fifth evaluation metric to the grid require running any new discovery cells?
items.answer: No. Metrics are applied to already-discovered circuits; specifications go from 1,540 x 12 to 1,540 x 15 while the 1,540 discovery cells stay the same.
rubric: Says no new discovery cells are needed
Explains that the metric is applied after discovery (the 1,540 vs 18,480 structure)

items.question: Would adding a sixth seed to the grid require running new discovery cells?
items.answer: Yes. The seed selects the sampled prompts that discovery runs on, so it is part of the discovery cell. It would add 308 new cells (7 x 22 x 2).
rubric: Says yes
Explains that the seed is a discovery-cell axis (prompt sampling), adding 308 cells

items.question: Would adding an eighth ablation operator that never reads the corrupt distribution add exactly 70 discovery cells?
items.answer: Yes. Such an operator is not crossed with the corruptions, so it adds 7 objectives x 2 prompts x 5 seeds = 70 cells.
rubric: Says yes, 70
Explains that it is not crossed with the 4 corruption levels, being like the two existing non-reading operators

items.question: Would adding an eighth ablation operator that does read the corrupt distribution add exactly 70 discovery cells?
items.answer: No. It would be crossed with the 4 corruption levels, adding 7 x 4 x 2 x 5 = 280 cells.
rubric: Says no
Explains nesting of the 4 corruptions under corruption-reading operators, giving 280

items.question: If region attribution still disagreed across size-matched specifications with size removed from the statement, could the disagreement be attributed to the size channel?
items.answer: No. Size has been held fixed and removed from the statement, so persisting disagreement must come through some other channel.
rubric: Says no
Explains that the control eliminates size as the route of disagreement

items.question: If region attribution agreed across size-matched specifications once size was removed from the statement, would the size channel be implicated in the overall claim flips?
items.answer: Yes. The pooled flips would then be explained by analytic choices changing circuit size, which the paper identifies as a hidden channel.
rubric: Says yes
Explains that disagreement vanishing under size control points to size as the propagating channel

items.question: In a size range where statement disagreement exceeds chance-corrected functional disagreement, is the claim map under-reporting the differences between mechanisms?
items.answer: No. There it is amplifying differences the mechanisms do not carry, which is the regime the paper labels 'filings differ more than mechanisms'.
rubric: Says no; the map amplifies rather than under-reports
Ties this to statements differing more than kappa-based functional disagreement

items.question: In a size range where chance-corrected functional disagreement exceeds statement disagreement, is the claim map under-reporting the differences between mechanisms?
items.answer: Yes. The statement procedure is coarser than the mechanisms there, so distinct mechanisms get compatible statements.
rubric: Says yes
Explains that the procedure is coarser than the mechanisms in that regime

items.question: A provider files a single circuit with its config and a pooled faithfulness score, and nothing else. Which protocol items are still missing?
items.answer: Missing are: the declared specification space with citations (1), the deterministic claim-map code (2), the reason the specification was selected (3, which needs more than the config), per-level discard rates (4), and the within-size decomposition of the pooled score (5).
rubric: Lists the specification space, claim-map code, selection rationale and discard rates as missing
Notes that the pooled score needs a within-group or within-size decomposition

items.question: A filer is drafting the account owed to a person under Article 86(1). What content should it lead with, and why not the overseer's version?
items.answer: It should lead with which parts of the input drove the decision, because the right is owed to the person the decision concerns. The overseer's account leads with where the behaviour sits and how concentrated it is, which may be inadequate for that person.
rubric: Says it should lead with input segments or input parts that drove the decision
Contrasts this with the overseer's location and concentration focus, which serves a different addressee

items.question: A conformity body proposes mandating a single faithfulness metric for all circuit filings. Given the paper's results, should it expect filed statements to become compatible?
items.answer: No. No single axis rescues the filing, and six axes would remain free. The axis that changes statements most need not be the metric, so any standard should be checked at the statement level.
rubric: Says no or not necessarily
Cites the 'no axis rescues' result or the six remaining free axes
Notes that standardisation should be evaluated at the statement level

items.question: A neuroscience multiverse study selects brain-region clusters by a significance threshold, so cluster size varies by specification. What does this paper recommend for its pooled statistics?
items.answer: Report every pooled statistic with its within-size decomposition. Size is an outcome of the threshold rather than an axis, so it can carry analytic choices into the results as a hidden channel.
rubric: Recommends within-size decomposition of pooled statistics
Explains that size is a threshold-determined outcome acting as a hidden channel

items.question: An analyst finds a within-group bootstrap interval for a three-specification group embarrassingly wide. What should they do under the paper's principles?
items.answer: They should report the point estimate with diagnostics. They should not construct a bias-corrected estimator in response to the unwelcome interval, because that would be the analytic flexibility the paper warns against.
rubric: Says to report a point estimate with diagnostics
Says not to devise a new estimator post hoc, because that is undisclosed flexibility

items.question: A team reruns the design with a library that also implements optimal ablation. Should they expect a narrower or wider space of filed statements than the GPT-2 grid, and why?
items.answer: Wider, or at least no narrower. An additional defensible operator expands the space, which is why the paper calls its library-bounded conclusions conservative.
rubric: Says wider or at least as wide
Explains that an added defensible level expands the space, consistent with the 'conservative' framing

items.question: A provider of a 70B-parameter system wants to cite the three-quarters flip rate as its expected instability. Is that justified?
items.answer: No. The study covers one small model on one task, and the paper says it is not obvious in which direction a larger circuit and statement space would move the result. The provider would need its own declared multiverse.
rubric: Says not justified
Explains that the result is limited to one model and one task and that the direction of scale effects is untested

items.question: If region attribution had agreed in the size-matched, size-removed comparison, which conclusion about Annex IV 2(b) accounts would lose its support?
items.answer: The conclusion that even the size-independent core of a general-logic account, namely where in the model the behaviour is located, varies across defensible specifications. The flips could instead be traced to the size channel.
rubric: Identifies the persistence-under-maximum-pressure conclusion about region attribution
Notes that the disagreement would be attributable to size instead

items.question: If holding one axis fixed had reduced claim flips to near zero, which conclusion would be undermined, and what would it imply for regulators?
items.answer: The 'no analytic axis rescues the filing' result would be undermined. Standardising that one axis would become a viable route, reducing the need for full specification-space disclosure.
rubric: Identifies the 'no axis rescues' result
Notes that single-axis standardisation would become viable

items.question: If circuits had shared most of their edges across specifications, would the claim-flip result automatically lose support?
items.answer: No. Structural overlap and statement compatibility are distinct, and overlapping circuits may still support different statements. Only the structural premise (c1) would change.
rubric: Says no
Explains that structure and statements are distinct units of analysis

items.question: If chance-corrected functional agreement had been high across the whole size range while statements still flipped, how would the reading of the claim-flip result change?
items.answer: The phantom specialisation objection would gain ground: the circuits would share a mechanism. The flips would then reflect the claim map amplifying differences everywhere, rather than discovery returning different mechanisms over part of the range.
rubric: Says the flips would be read as amplification by the statement procedure, or phantom specialisation, rather than mechanism differences
Notes that the 'over part of the range' finding would become the whole range

items.question: If the Pythia-160m replication met its pre-registered refutation criteria, which conclusions would it weaken and which would remain?
items.answer: It would weaken any extension of the findings beyond GPT-2 small or to other architectures. The GPT-2 IOI results themselves would stand, since the paper claims nothing beyond one model and one task.
rubric: Says it weakens generalisation to other models or architectures
Says the GPT-2 IOI findings themselves are not overturned

items.question: If the specification curve showed each region statement supported only by specifications sharing one particular axis level, which other result would be in tension with that pattern?
items.answer: The 'no analytic axis rescues the filing' result. Statements tied to a single axis level would mean fixing that axis would make statements agree.
rubric: Identifies the 'no axis rescues' result
Explains that statements tied to one axis level imply single-axis standardisation would work

items.question: Which protocol item exists specifically because of the hazard identified for the random baseline?
items.answer: Item 5: report any pooled statistic with its within-group decomposition, particularly within circuit size. Pooled baseline directions can mislead because of size mixing.
rubric: Identifies item 5 (within-group or within-size decomposition)
Links it to size-mixing in pooled baseline comparisons

items.question: Does the near-disjointness of circuits show that circuit discovery fails to recover genuine structure? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Structurally distinct circuits can implement the same computation, as phantom specialisation shows, and the paper disclaims any bearing on whether discovery recovers genuine structure.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites structural difference not implying functional difference, or the paper's explicit disclaimer

items.question: Does the paper show that nondeterminism in discovery algorithms is a main driver of circuit instability? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The seed axis selects sampled prompts, so it measures evaluation-set variability rather than nondeterminism, and it is only one of seven axes.
rubric: Answers not settled
Explains that the seed captures prompt sampling, not algorithmic nondeterminism

items.question: Does the paper support excluding interpretability evidence from technical documentation? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The protocol is designed to accompany such evidence with disclosure of its specification space, not to remove it.
rubric: Answers contradicted
Explains that the remedy is disclosure alongside the evidence, not exclusion

items.question: Does the paper show that claim instability spans the full set of defensible choices in the interpretability literature? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The grid is only as wide as the library; optimal ablation, for example, is excluded. The results are therefore a conservative view, not a census of the literature's space.
rubric: Answers not settled
Cites the library-bounded grid or the optimal ablation omission

items.question: Does the paper show that the same instability would arise for other tasks on GPT-2 small? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Only IOI was run; a second task is designed but not run.
rubric: Answers not settled
Notes that only one task was run and the second task is unrun

items.question: Does the paper show that the axis causing the most edge-set variation is the best one to standardise? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted as a general rule. The axes governing structure need not govern statements, so standardising the most structure-changing axis could leave the statement-changing axis free.
rubric: Answers contradicted, or not supported
Explains the structure/statement axis mismatch and that standardisation should be judged at the statement level

items.question: Suppose the claim map's size categories were picked by hand after the analyst had looked at the discovered circuits. Would the resulting claim-flip rate still be interpretable as evidence about variation across specifications, and why?
items.answer: No. A hand-picked discretisation is itself an undeclared analytic choice made after seeing the data. The flip rate could then reflect where the analyst drew the category boundaries rather than how circuits vary across specifications. The paper requires categories from a committed calibration rule applied to a measured curve, with sensitivity reported and the discretisation declared in the specification space.
rubric: Asserts the flip rate would no longer be cleanly interpretable (or would be compromised).
Reason: the hand-picked category boundaries are an undeclared, post-hoc analytic choice that can drive the statements and so the flips.
Condition/remedy: categories must come from a committed calibration rule, with sensitivity reported and the discretisation declared as part of the specification space.

items.question: The paper's warning about the random baseline rests on what happens at large circuit sizes. Would that specific degeneracy still arise in a model whose graph is so large that a size-matched random draw never touches every component, even at the largest admitted sizes?
items.answer: No, not that specific degeneracy. It arises because a random draw that touches every component can support only one statement. If draws never cover all components, random subsets can still map to different statements. The within-size comparison remains the recommended practice, but the reason the baseline collapses at large sizes would not apply.
rubric: Asserts the specific degeneracy would not arise (the baseline would not collapse to a single statement).
Reason: the degeneracy depends on random draws touching every component, which forces one statement; draws that leave components untouched can still yield varied statements.

items.question: The deviations file records whether each deviation was decided before or after the affected material was seen. If that before/after field were dropped, what protection would the pre-registration lose?
items.answer: Readers could no longer tell whether a change was made in response to results. That would hide exactly the kind of data-dependent analytic flexibility the paper studies. The study's own conclusions could then not be distinguished from flexibility-manufactured ones, and a study about analytic flexibility that was itself flexible would undermine its own argument.
rubric: Asserts readers could no longer distinguish result-driven (post hoc) changes from pre-planned ones.
Reason: undisclosed post hoc changes are exactly the analytic flexibility the paper warns about, so the study's conclusions could be self-undermining.

items.question: Suppose some threshold settings admitted discovered circuits so large that each touched every component. Would high agreement among those circuits' region statements count as evidence of filability, and why?
items.answer: No. A circuit that touches every component maps to a single region statement, just as the large random draw does. Agreement there is forced by the mapping and size rather than by convergent mechanisms. The agreement is degenerate and uninformative about whether competent analysts would reach compatible accounts.
rubric: Asserts the agreement would not be evidence of filability.
Reason: circuits touching every component can support only one statement, so agreement is guaranteed by size/the mapping (degenerate), as with the large-size random baseline.

items.question: Suppose the pool of IOI prompts the seed axis samples from were so small that different seeds drew nearly identical prompt sets. What would the seed axis then measure, and could it shed light on algorithmic nondeterminism?
items.answer: It would capture almost no evaluation-set variability, because the seed only selects which prompts are sampled. It would contribute little variation to the grid. Its weak effect would also say nothing about nondeterminism, since the seed axis never measured nondeterminism in the first place.
rubric: Asserts the seed axis would measure little or no variation (near-identical evaluation sets).
Reason: the seed only selects sampled prompts (evaluation-set variability), so it cannot speak to algorithmic nondeterminism either way.

items.question: Why does a claim flip at the coarsest granularity imply that the two specifications' statements also disagree at every finer granularity?
items.answer: The granularities are nested, so a finer statement refines the coarser one rather than contradicting it. Two finer statements that refine incompatible coarse statements cannot be compatible. Coarse disagreement therefore propagates to every level of detail.
rubric: Asserts that coarse disagreement entails disagreement at all finer levels.
Reason: granularities are nested; finer statements refine (do not contradict) the coarse statement, so they inherit the coarse incompatibility.

items.question: In the Section 7.4 control, why is it not enough to strip size-dependent content from the statement? Why must the comparison also be restricted to same-size circuits?
items.answer: Size can still shape the region attribution itself. Larger circuits touch more of the network, as the random baseline shows when large draws touch every component. Removing size wording from the statement would leave size acting as a hidden channel. Only matching size closes that channel.
rubric: Asserts size can influence region attribution even after size wording is removed.
Reason: larger circuits cover more components/regions (cf. random draws touching everything), so size is a hidden channel that only size matching removes.

items.question: Why can the same pair of circuits flip the claim for one addressee but not for the other?
items.answer: The two addressees' statements lead with different content. The overseer's statement covers where the behaviour is carried and how concentrated it is. The affected person's statement covers which input parts drove the decision. Two circuits can agree on one kind of content and disagree on the other.
rubric: Asserts the two addressee statements can diverge in agreement because they report different content.
Reason: the overseer statement concerns location and concentration in the network; the Article 86 statement concerns which input parts drove the decision.

items.question: Why is complying with the filability protocol cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit?
items.answer: Everything the protocol asks for is already produced by, or computed from, the sweep's stored outputs: the declared space, discard rates and within-size decompositions. The claim map is deterministic code, and the analysis layer runs without a GPU. Disclosure therefore needs no new discovery runs.
rubric: Asserts compliance requires no new expensive discovery computation.
Reason: the required items come from the sweep's existing outputs, with a deterministic claim map and an analysis layer that runs without a GPU.

items.question: Why does it matter that the claim map, and not only the discovery grid, was fixed before any confirmatory work?
items.answer: Claim flips are defined through the mapping from circuit to statement. If the mapping had been adjusted after seeing circuits, the flip rate could be tuned up or down. That would reintroduce analytic flexibility at the statement layer, which the study is meant to expose rather than exercise.
rubric: Asserts that a post hoc claim map could make the flip rate an artefact of tuning.
Reason: flips are computed through the mapping, so choosing it after seeing circuits is analytic flexibility at the statement level.

items.question: Why can two circuits with little edge overlap still support the same region statement under the claim map?
items.answer: The claim map aggregates edges up to statements about regions, concentration or input segments. Different edges lying in the same region can therefore yield the same statement. Edge-level disjointness need not show up at the coarser level of what is filed.
rubric: Asserts that low edge overlap is compatible with identical statements.
Reason: the statement aggregates edges into coarser units (regions etc.), so different edges in the same region map to the same claim.

items.question: If two specifications' statements agree at the finest granularity, must they also agree at the coarsest granularity?
items.answer: Yes. Finer statements refine the coarser ones in the nested hierarchy, so agreeing fine statements imply the same coarse statement.
rubric: Answers yes.
Reason: nesting means each fine statement determines (refines) a unique coarse statement.

items.question: If two specifications' statements agree at the coarsest granularity, must they also agree at the finest granularity?
items.answer: No. A coarse region statement can be refined in different ways, for example in how distributed the computation is or which input segment it reads, so the finer statements can still differ.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: finer levels add information (distribution, input segment) on which statements sharing a coarse claim can still differ.

items.question: At circuit sizes where a uniform random draw touches every component, can size-matched random subsets passed through the claim map disagree with one another on the statement?
items.answer: No. Such draws touch every component and can support only one statement, so the baseline is degenerate there.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: touching every component forces a single statement (degenerate baseline).

items.question: At sizes small enough that a uniform random draw leaves some components untouched, can size-matched random subsets disagree with one another on the statement?
items.answer: Yes. Different draws can touch different components or regions and so map to different statements. The degeneracy is specific to large sizes.
rubric: Answers yes.
Reason: draws that leave components untouched can cover different regions, so the mapping can yield different statements.

items.question: Is a bootstrap that resamples specifications an acceptable way to quantify uncertainty in the pairwise claim-flip rate, under the paper's statistical approach?
items.answer: Yes, provided the interval is read as conditional on the designed grid rather than as licensing inference beyond it. Resampling specifications respects the dependence among pairs that share a specification.
rubric: Answers yes (acceptable).
Reason/condition: resampling specifications handles the dependence among pairs sharing specifications, and the interval is conditional on the grid.

items.question: Is a bootstrap that resamples pairs of specifications as independent units an acceptable way to quantify uncertainty in the claim-flip rate?
items.answer: No. Pairs that share a specification are dependent, so treating them as independent misrepresents the uncertainty, typically giving intervals that are too narrow.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: pairwise quantities are dependent whenever pairs share a specification, so resampling pairs as independent units is invalid (overstates precision).

items.question: For circuits of a few hundred edges in GPT-2 small's factorised graph, is the overlap expected between two random edge subsets of that size close to zero?
items.answer: Yes. A few hundred edges is a tiny fraction of tens of thousands, so random subsets of that size are expected to share almost nothing.
rubric: Answers yes.
Reason: the circuits are a very small fraction of a graph with tens of thousands of edges.

items.question: If the threshold rule admitted circuits covering most of the factorised graph, would two random edge subsets of that size still be expected to share almost nothing?
items.answer: No. Subsets that each cover most of the graph must overlap heavily, so chance overlap would be large and the comparison against chance would change accordingly.
rubric: Answers no.
Reason: when each subset covers most of the edge set, they necessarily share many edges, so chance overlap is high.

items.question: A team studies a model with ten times more edges than GPT-2 small and reports that its few-hundred-edge circuits share three times more edges than chance. How much should that reassure a regulator?
items.answer: Very little. In a bigger graph, chance overlap for same-size circuits is even closer to zero, so beating it is an even weaker bar. In any case, structural overlap is not the quantity a filing depends on; statement compatibility is.
rubric: Asserts the result is weak reassurance.
Reason: chance overlap shrinks as the graph grows, so exceeding it is an even weaker bar.
Adds that edge overlap is not what the filing depends on; statements are.

items.question: A provider runs many configurations and files the one whose region statement is most favourable to it. Which protocol items would make this visible to a second analyst?
items.answer: Item 1, declaring the specification space with citations, shows what else could have been run. Item 3, stating which specification produced the circuit and why it was selected, forces the selection rationale into the open. Together they let another analyst rerun the space and see that other defensible specifications support different statements.
rubric: Identifies item 1 (declared specification space) and item 3 (chosen specification and why).
Reason: together these expose the alternatives and the selection, so another analyst can reproduce the space and see the contrary statements.

items.question: A filer reports a single overall discard rate of 10% for its grid. Does that satisfy the protocol's discard item, and why?
items.answer: No. Item 4 requires the discard rate per axis level. A metric-relative threshold rule can admit circuits unevenly, so the discards could be concentrated under one metric. An overall rate would then hide a skewed composition of the surviving evidence.
rubric: Asserts it does not satisfy the protocol.

Reason: discards must be reported per axis level because a metric-relative threshold rule can concentrate discards in particular levels (e.g. one metric), skewing composition that an aggregate rate hides.

items.question: Two published analyses of the same model attribute a behaviour to different regions. Before treating this as a substantive scientific conflict, what does the paper imply a reader needs?
items.answer: The reader needs each analysis's declared specification space and chosen specification. With claims flipping on about three quarters of specification pairs, two defensible settings can easily produce opposite region attributions. Without the declared spaces, the conflict cannot be told apart from analytic variation.
rubric: Asserts the reader needs the declared specification spaces/chosen specifications of both analyses.
Reason: claims flip on most specification pairs, including region attribution, so the disagreement could stem from defensible analytic choices rather than a real conflict.

items.question: A standards body proposes fixing the threshold so that all filed circuits have comparable size, expecting this to make region attributions agree. Should it expect that, given the paper's results?
items.answer: No. Section 7.4 shows region attribution still varies among same-size circuits once size-dependent content is removed. Equalising size does not remove the disagreement, consistent with the finding that no single axis rescues the filing.
rubric: Asserts region attributions would still disagree.
Reason: the size-matched, size-removed comparison already shows region attribution varying among same-size circuits (and no single axis rescues the filing).

items.question: A filer's declared specification space lists only the single evaluation metric it actually used. Does that satisfy protocol item 1?
items.answer: No. Item 1 asks for the levels a competent analyst could defend, each with a citation, not just the level used. Published alternatives exist; the grid alone uses four metrics from the Miller et al. library. Listing only the chosen level hides the space the protocol is meant to reveal.
rubric: Asserts item 1 is not satisfied.
Reason: item 1 requires all defensible levels with citations; published alternative metrics exist (e.g. the four in the library), so a single level hides the space.

items.question: If the claim map's granularities were not nested, so that a finer statement could contradict a coarser one, which inference drawn from the coarsest-granularity flips would lose its force?
items.answer: The inference that disagreement at the coarsest, most lenient level carries through to every more detailed filing. Without nesting, a coarse flip would not guarantee fine-level disagreement. Nor would fine-level agreement imply coarse agreement, so the levels could not be read as one interpretable hierarchy.
rubric: Identifies the inference that coarse-level disagreement propagates to (rules out agreement at) finer levels / the interpretable hierarchy.
Reason: that propagation depends on finer statements refining rather than contradicting coarser ones.

items.question: If computing the within-size decompositions and discard rates had required rerunning discovery on GPUs, which of the paper's claims about the protocol would be weakened?
items.answer: The claims that the protocol is cheap relative to the sweep and satisfiable with existing tooling. Both rest on the analysis layer running without a GPU over stored outputs.
rubric: Identifies the cheapness / existing-tooling claim for the protocol.
Reason: that claim relies on disclosure quantities being computed from stored outputs by a GPU-free analysis layer.

items.question: If the relationship between statement disagreement and functional disagreement had been constant across circuit sizes, would protocol item 5 lose its justification?
items.answer: Only partly. It would lose the motivation from Section 7.6, that a pooled figure can hide which regime dominates in which part of the range. It would keep the motivation from Section 7.5, where pooled random-baseline comparisons mislead because the baseline becomes degenerate at large sizes.
rubric: Asserts item 5 would remain justified, losing only part of its motivation.
Reason: the Section 7.6 regime-mixing rationale would disappear, but the Section 7.5 random-baseline/size-degeneracy rationale would still require within-size decomposition.

items.question: Suppose size-matched random subsets passed through the claim map flipped as often as discovered circuits within every size. Which of the paper's filability conclusions would this undermine?
items.answer: None of them. The baseline answers only whether discovered circuits behave differently from arbitrary subgraphs, and the paper explicitly does not claim discovered circuits beat random. The claim-flip rate and the case for disclosure stand regardless.
rubric: Asserts the filability conclusions (claim flips, protocol) would not be undermined.
Reason: the baseline speaks only to discovered vs arbitrary subgraphs, which the paper explicitly makes no claim about.

items.question: Suppose the Pythia-160m replication reproduced the overall claim-flip rate, but region attribution agreed in its size-matched, size-removed comparison. Which conclusion would then look specific to GPT-2 small?
items.answer: The maximum-pressure conclusion, that disagreement cannot be attributed to the size channel. On Pythia the flips could be explained by size, so the persistence of region disagreement beyond size would appear model-specific.
rubric: Identifies the maximum-pressure / not-attributable-to-size conclusion (Section 7.4).
Reason: on Pythia, disagreement would vanish once size is matched and removed, implicating the size channel there.

items.question: If chance-corrected, example-level agreement had been low for structurally distinct circuits across the entire size range, what would happen to the phantom specialisation objection and to the finding that filings differ more than mechanisms?
items.answer: The objection would fail for this grid, because the circuits would genuinely differ in mechanism rather than being members of one equivalence class. The finding that statements differ more than mechanisms over part of the range would also lose support, since mechanisms would differ at least as much everywhere.
rubric: Asserts the phantom specialisation objection would fail (circuits are functionally different, not an equivalence class).
Asserts the 'filings differ more than mechanisms over part of the range' result would lose support, because functional disagreement would be high throughout.

items.question: Does Section 7.4 show that Article 86 statements about which input parts drove a decision remain unstable among size-matched circuits? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The control reduces the statement to region attribution, the core of an Annex IV 2(b) overseer-facing account. Input-part content for the affected person is not what that control tests.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the Section 7.4 control reduces statements to region attribution (Annex IV 2(b)), not the input-part content owed under Article 86.

items.question: Does the paper's bootstrap interval for the claim-flip rate bound the instability one would see if optimal ablation were added as an operator? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Intervals resample specifications within the designed grid and are conditional on it, not licensing inference beyond it. Optimal ablation is not in the library, so it never entered the grid.
rubric: Answers contradicted (the paper rules out such inference).
Reason: intervals are conditional on the grid, and optimal ablation was excluded because the library does not implement it.

items.question: If the pre-registered Pythia-160m replication succeeds, would the paper's findings be shown to hold at larger scale? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Pythia-160m is a small model of a different architecture family performing the same task. A successful replication would address model-specificity, not scale, and the paper claims nothing about scale.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the replication changes architecture family at a comparably small size, so it tests model-specificity rather than scale, about which the paper claims nothing.

items.question: Does the paper show that its statement procedure amplifies differences the mechanisms do not carry across the whole circuit-size range? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. Statement disagreement exceeds chance-corrected functional disagreement only over part of the range, and the relationship varies with size. Elsewhere the procedure can be coarser than the mechanisms.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Reason: the excess of statement over functional disagreement holds only over part of the size range; the relationship varies with size.

items.question: Does the filability protocol let a regulator determine which of two conflicting filed circuits is correct? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The protocol is designed so that the regulator does not adjudicate which analytic choice is correct. It only requires the filer to declare the space and its choice, so a second analyst can reproduce or challenge the account on equal terms.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Reason: the protocol deliberately avoids adjudicating correctness and instead enables reproduction/challenge via declared space and choice.

items.question: Does the paper show that the evaluation metric is the axis responsible for most of the statement disagreement? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The metric is named as the obvious candidate because of prior sensitivity and inflation results, but the paper does not rank it as the main driver. It reports that holding any single axis fixed does not remove the disagreement, and that standardising the metric would leave six axes free.
rubric: Answers not settled (the paper does not establish it).
Reason: the metric is only the obvious candidate from prior work; the paper finds no single axis rescues the filing and gives no ranking making the metric dominant.

items.question: A filer files the circuit from whichever specification in its sweep scored highest on sufficiency. Would that high sufficiency score show that the filed account is filable?
items.answer: No. Sufficiency is one of the metrics Hsia et al. show can be inflated, and the paper treats the metric as one analytic axis among seven, not a neutral measuring device. Filability asks whether other defensible specifications yield compatible statements, and a score on one specification says nothing about that. Picking by score is itself a selection the filer would have to state and justify under protocol item 3.
rubric: Says no, the score does not establish filability.
Reason: filability concerns agreement of statements across the declared specification space, not one configuration's score, and/or sufficiency is an inflatable metric that is itself an analytic axis.
Notes that the selection rule must be disclosed (protocol item 3) or is the kind of undisclosed flexibility the paper warns about.

items.question: The claim map's size categories come from a committed calibration rule, but the filer reports nothing about how statements change under other calibration choices. What would a reviewer then be unable to tell?
items.answer: The reviewer could not tell whether the observed agreement or flips depend on the discretisation itself rather than on the circuits. Every discretisation between circuit and statement is an analytic choice that belongs in the specification space. A committed rule removes hand-picking, but without a sensitivity report the effect of that choice stays hidden.
rubric: Says the reviewer could not tell whether statement agreement or flips are driven by the size-category discretisation rather than by the circuits.
Reason: the discretisation is itself an analytic choice in the specification space, and committing to a rule does not reveal its influence; the paper asks for sensitivity to be reported.

items.question: Suppose the grid's cells had been run across several different software environments instead of one pinned environment. Could differences between seeds still be read purely as evaluation-set variability?
items.answer: No. The seed only selects which prompts are sampled. Differences between environments could add variation that no declared axis captures, and that variation would be confounded with the seed and other axes. The single pinned environment and the environment fingerprint are what keep variation attributable to the declared axes.
rubric: Says no.
Reason: differences between environments would add an undeclared source of variation, confounded with the seed (and other) axes; the pinned environment is what isolates the seed as prompt sampling.

items.question: If corruption had been crossed with all seven ablation operators instead of nested, in which direction would the resulting duplicate specifications bias the pairwise claim-flip rate, and why?
items.answer: The rate would be biased downward. The two operators that never read the corrupt distribution would each be run under four corruption labels and would return identical circuits. Pairs of these duplicates would always support the same statement, so they would add pairs that never flip and make the filing look more stable than the distinct specifications warrant.
rubric: Says the claim-flip rate would be biased downward (apparent stability inflated).
Reason: the duplicate specifications for operators that ignore the corrupt distribution produce identical circuits, so pairs among them never flip.

items.question: Two specifications differ only in seed, so each sampled a different set of IOI prompts. If each circuit's successes and failures were taken on its own sampled prompts, could the Section 7.6 functional-agreement measure be computed validly?
items.answer: No. The measure compares, example by example, whether two circuits succeed and fail on the same inputs. On disjoint or different prompt sets there are no shared examples to pair, so neither raw agreement nor kappa means anything. Both circuits must be evaluated on a common set of inputs.
rubric: Says no, the measure would not be valid.
Reason: example-level agreement (and kappa) requires both circuits to be scored on the same inputs; the seed changes which prompts are sampled.

items.question: A filer tried a published ablation operator, saw that it supported a different region statement, and left that operator out of its declared specification space. Would the protocol still let a second analyst reproduce or challenge the account on equal terms?
items.answer: No. The protocol depends on item 1 declaring every level a competent analyst could defend. Omitting a tried level that disagrees hides exactly the part of the space that would reveal the instability. The second analyst would be working in a narrower space than the one the filer actually explored, so the account is asserted rather than audited.
rubric: Says no.
Reason: item 1 requires declaring all defensible levels; omitting one that changes the statement conceals the disagreement, so the second analyst does not work on equal terms.

items.question: Why does the verification script compute pairwise quantities by more than one route, including a brute-force computation, rather than relying on one efficient implementation?
items.answer: The headline results, such as the claim-flip rate, are pairwise quantities over very many specifications, and an efficient computation can hide implementation errors. Recomputing the same quantity by an independent brute-force route checks that the reported numbers really follow from the stored outputs and are not artefacts of code.
rubric: Says independent routes guard against implementation errors in computing the pairwise quantities.
Links this to the headline results being pairwise (e.g. the claim-flip rate) and being checked against stored raw outputs.

items.question: Why can changing only the evaluation metric change which specification pairs enter the Section 7.4 size-matched comparison?
items.answer: Circuit size is not set by the analyst. It is an outcome of the threshold rule, and that rule is metric-relative. A different metric can therefore admit circuits of different sizes, which changes which specifications have same-size partners in the matched comparison.
rubric: Says the metric changes the size of the admitted circuits.
Reason: size is an outcome of the metric-relative threshold rule, so it determines which pairs are size-matched.

items.question: Why can discovered circuits still support different statements at sizes where a size-matched uniform random draw has become degenerate?
items.answer: The random baseline is degenerate because a uniform draw of that many edges spreads across the graph and touches every component. Discovered circuits are not uniform draws: discovery concentrates edges in selected components. At the same size they can therefore leave components untouched and differ in which region they emphasise.
rubric: Identifies that the degeneracy comes from uniform sampling spreading edges over every component.
Reason: discovery selects edges non-uniformly and concentrates them, so discovered circuits of the same size need not touch every component and can differ in region.

items.question: Why does the paper treat building a bias-corrected estimator, in response to an unwelcome bootstrap interval for a small group, as the very behaviour it warns against?
items.answer: Choosing an estimator after seeing an unwelcome result is a post-hoc analytic choice. That is the undisclosed flexibility which, as Simmons et al. showed, lets an analyst present almost anything. It would also depart from the pre-registered plan, and a study about analytic flexibility must not itself be flexible. The pre-registered response is to report point estimates with diagnostics.
rubric: Says it is a post-hoc analytic choice driven by the result, i.e. undisclosed analytic flexibility.

Reason ties to self-consistency or pre-registration: a study of analytic flexibility that adjusts its analysis after seeing results would undermine its own argument (the alternative is point estimates with diagnostics).

items.question: Why does protocol item 1 require a citation for each declared level of each axis?
items.answer: In the paper, a level counts as defensible because it comes from a published implementation; the grid contains no invented levels. A citation lets a regulator check that each level has that standing without judging which choice is correct. The space is then anchored in the literature rather than in the filer's say-so, which keeps the protocol free of adjudication.
rubric: Says citations ground each level's defensibility in published work, mirroring the grid's rule that every level comes from a published implementation.
Reason: this lets the regulator verify the space without adjudicating which analytic choice is correct.

items.question: Why does stripping size-dependent content in the Section 7.4 control leave region attribution but remove the overseer's account of how concentrated the computation is?
items.answer: How concentrated the responsible computation is depends directly on how many edges or components the circuit contains, and that size is set by the threshold rule. Where the behaviour is located can be stated independently of size. So removing size-dependent content leaves only the region attribution, the Annex IV 2(b) core.
rubric: Says concentration is size-dependent content, whereas region attribution can be stated independently of size.
Reason: concentration reflects how many edges or components the circuit includes, which is set by the threshold rule.

items.question: Two circuits each succeed on 50% of IOI examples and agree on 90% of examples. Does their agreement exceed what accuracy alone would produce?
items.answer: Yes. With both circuits at 50% accuracy, chance agreement is 0.5×0.5 + 0.5×0.5 = 0.5. Observed agreement of 0.9 gives a kappa of (0.9 − 0.5)/0.5 = 0.8, well above chance.
rubric: Says yes, agreement exceeds chance.
Reason: expected chance agreement is about 50%, so 90% gives a high chance-corrected agreement (kappa about 0.8).

items.question: Two circuits each succeed on 95% of IOI examples and agree on 90% of examples. Does their agreement exceed what accuracy alone would produce?
items.answer: No. Chance agreement is 0.95×0.95 + 0.05×0.05 ≈ 0.905. Observed agreement of 0.90 is at or slightly below that, so kappa is about zero or slightly negative.
rubric: Says no, agreement does not exceed chance.
Reason: expected chance agreement is about 90.5%, so 90% observed gives kappa near zero (or negative).

items.question: Under the pre-registered exclusion rules, is a specification for which the threshold rule admits no circuit recorded as a discard?
items.answer: Yes. Specifications for which the threshold rule admits no circuit are one of the two pre-registered exclusions. They are recorded as discards with their rates and are not repaired.
rubric: Says yes, it is recorded as a discard.
Reason: this is one of the two exclusions fixed in advance (alongside execution failures), recorded with rates and not repaired.

items.question: Under the pre-registered exclusion rules, is a specification that admits a circuit, but whose statement contradicts the filer's preferred account, recorded as a discard?
items.answer: No. The only exclusions are cells that fail to execute and specifications with no admitted circuit, and both criteria were fixed before any circuit was seen. Excluding a specification because of what its statement says would be the result-driven flexibility the study warns against.
rubric: Says no.
Reason: exclusions are limited to execution failures and no admitted circuit, fixed before circuits were seen; excluding by statement content would be result-driven flexibility.

items.question: A discovery cell is rerun in the pinned environment with the same configuration and the same seed. Should it return the same circuit?
items.answer: Yes. The seed selects which prompts are sampled and does not represent nondeterminism. Every run traces to a config, a seed and an environment fingerprint, so the same configuration, seed and environment should reproduce the same prompts and the same circuit.
rubric: Says yes.
Reason: the seed fixes the prompt sample and is not nondeterminism, and config, seed and environment fully trace a run.

items.question: A discovery cell is rerun in the pinned environment with the same configuration but a different seed. Should it be expected to return the same circuit?
items.answer: Not necessarily. A different seed samples different prompts, and the seed axis exists to measure evaluation-set variability. The circuit can change because the evaluation set changed.
rubric: Says not necessarily, or that it may differ.
Reason: a different seed selects different prompts, so the axis captures evaluation-set variability.

items.question: If every discovered circuit and its matched random subsets had exactly the same size across all specifications, would a pooled baseline comparison be interpretable without a within-size decomposition?
items.answer: Yes. With a single size, the pooled comparison is the within-size comparison. The hazard the paper identifies comes from mixing different distributions of circuit size, and that cannot happen here.
rubric: Says yes.
Reason: with one size the pooled comparison equals the within-size comparison; the hazard comes from mixing size distributions.

items.question: If specifications admitted circuits across a wide range of sizes, including sizes where a uniform random draw touches every component, would a pooled baseline comparison be interpretable without a within-size decomposition?
items.answer: No. The pooled comparison would mix size distributions, including a region where the baseline is degenerate and supports only one statement. Its direction could then point either way for reasons unrelated to discovery quality, so it is uninterpretable without the within-size decomposition.
rubric: Says no.
Reason: pooling mixes size distributions, including the degenerate large-size region, so the direction can mislead regardless of discovery quality.

items.question: A filer produces its statement with its published deterministic claim map, then has a language model rephrase the statement for readability before filing. Does the filed text satisfy protocol item 2?
items.answer: No. Item 2 requires the procedure from circuit to filed statement to be deterministic, published code, not a language model. The rephrased text is no longer what the published map outputs, and it brings in model variance that cannot be separated from circuit variance. A second analyst running the map could not reproduce the filed wording.
rubric: Says no.

Reason: the filed statement is no longer the output of the declared deterministic map, and the language model adds variance that is inseparable from circuit variance, so the statement cannot be reproduced.

items.question: The Pythia-160m replication keeps four metrics and three thresholds. How many specifications does it contain?
items.answer: 11,088. Specifications are discovery cells multiplied by metrics and thresholds, as in the GPT-2 grid where 1,540 × 12 = 18,480, so 924 × 4 × 3 = 11,088.
rubric: Gives 11,088.
Reason: specifications = discovery cells × 4 metrics × 3 thresholds (924 × 12).

items.question: A team runs a multiverse in which every specification keeps exactly the top 300 edges, whatever the metric. Does circuit size still act as a hidden channel in their pooled statistics?
items.answer: No. Size is then fixed by the analyst and constant across specifications, so pooled statistics coincide with within-size ones. The value 300 is now an analytic choice and should be declared in the specification space. On the paper's evidence, fixing size would not by itself remove disagreement about region.
rubric: Says size no longer acts as a hidden channel.
Reason: size is constant and set by the analyst rather than an outcome of the threshold rule, so pooled equals within-size.
Notes that the fixed size is itself an analytic choice to declare, and/or that matched size did not remove region disagreement in Section 7.4.

items.question: Two providers file region statements about the same model, each derived through its own claim map, and the statements disagree. What does the paper imply is needed before the disagreement can be blamed on the circuits?
items.answer: Both claim maps must be available as published deterministic code. The derivation procedure is part of the evidence, and its discretisations are analytic choices. The disagreement could come from the maps rather than the circuits, so both circuits need to go through the same map to separate the two.
rubric: Says both claim maps are needed as published code (or both circuits must be run through a common map).
Reason: the map from circuit to statement is part of the evidence, and its choices (e.g. discretisations) can produce disagreement on their own.

items.question: A conformity body proposes that providers must file the statement supported by the largest share of their declared specification space, instead of the one from their chosen specification. Is that something the paper's protocol requires?
items.answer: No. The protocol requires declaring the space, the deterministic claim map, the chosen specification and why it was selected, discard rates, and within-group decompositions. It deliberately does not prescribe which choice is right. A mandated selection rule goes beyond that disclosure-only design.
rubric: Says no, the protocol does not require this.
Reason: the protocol only requires disclosure of the space and of the chosen specification with its rationale (item 3); it avoids prescribing or adjudicating the correct choice.

items.question: A second analyst reruns a filed configuration with the same config and seed and gets a different circuit. Given the paper's reproducibility setup, where should they look for the cause?
items.answer: They should compare the environment fingerprint and the code commit. The commit can be recovered by content-addressed comparison of archived outputs against the git tree. The seed only selects prompts and is not a source of nondeterminism, so a mismatch at the same config and seed points to a different environment or code version.
rubric: Says to check the environment fingerprint and/or code commit (version).
Reason: with config and seed equal and the seed only selecting prompts, the remaining traced inputs (environment, code) must account for the difference.

items.question: A provider adds a prompt variant it wrote itself and has never published. Under the paper's rules, can that variant enter the declared specification space as a defensible level?
items.answer: Not as things stand. Protocol item 1 requires a citation for each level, and the paper's own grid admits only levels taken from published implementations. An unpublished variant has no such grounding, so its defensibility cannot be checked without the regulator judging it.
rubric: Says no, not as a defensible level.
Reason: levels must carry a citation to published work (item 1, and the grid's rule of published levels only), which an unpublished variant lacks.

items.question: Suppose the threshold rule had admitted circuits at equal rates for every metric and no cell had failed to execute. Which stated limitation would become moot for this grid, and would protocol item 4 still be worth requiring?
items.answer: The limitation that the discard rule shapes the evidence would be moot, because the surviving pool would keep the balanced composition. Item 4 would still be worth requiring: a filer cannot assume this in general, and the paper asks filings to record which configurations ran and which did not. A zero discard rate per level is itself the report that makes the composition visible.
rubric: Identifies the 'discard rule shapes the evidence' limitation (uneven composition of the surviving pool) as moot.
Says item 4 is still worth requiring, because composition must be shown rather than assumed (zero rates are themselves the disclosure).

items.question: If chance-corrected functional agreement had been near perfect across the whole size range, so that all circuits implemented the same mechanism, would the filability protocol lose its justification?
items.answer: No. What is filed is the statement, and statements still flip on about three quarters of pairs. A second analyst would therefore still file something incompatible. The instability would be traced to the statement procedure amplifying differences, which makes publishing the claim map and declaring the space more important, not less.
rubric: Says no, the protocol would still be justified.
Reason: filability concerns statements, which still flip; with mechanisms agreeing the flips come from the procedure, which strengthens the need to disclose the claim map and the space.

items.question: Which hazard identified for the random baseline also applies when comparing statement disagreement with functional disagreement, and what does it require there?
items.answer: Circuit size acting as a hidden channel. The relationship between statement and functional disagreement varies with size, so a pooled figure can hide which regime dominates in which part of the range. The comparison should be reported within size, as protocol item 5 requires for pooled statistics.
rubric: Identifies the circuit-size channel, i.e. that pooling across sizes misleads.
Says the statement-versus-functional comparison must be decomposed within size, because the regime varies with size.

items.question: If the random edge subsets had been mapped to statements by a different procedure from the one applied to discovered circuits, which question could the baseline no longer answer?
items.answer: It could no longer answer whether discovered circuits behave differently from arbitrary subgraphs of matched size. Any difference in statement agreement could then come from the two procedures rather than from discovery, because the statement procedure is part of the evidence.
rubric: Says the baseline could no longer show whether discovered circuits differ from arbitrary subgraphs.
Reason: differences in statements could be caused by the differing procedures rather than by discovery.

items.question: If Section 7.1 had found circuits nearly identical in their edges across specifications, would the phantom specialisation objection still need addressing for the claim-flip result?
items.answer: No, it would be largely moot. The objection is that structurally distinct circuits may implement the same computation. Nearly identical circuits passed through a deterministic claim map would yield nearly identical statements, leaving no flips for the objection to explain away.
rubric: Says it would be largely moot or would not need addressing.
Reason: the objection concerns structurally distinct circuits; nearly identical circuits under a deterministic map would support the same statements.

items.question: If claim flips had occurred only in the affected person's statement and never in region attribution, which results would lose support?
items.answer: The Section 7.4 result would lose support, since it says region attribution still varies among size-matched circuits with size removed from the statement. So would the part of the claim-flip result saying flips include substantive disagreement about which region is responsible. The Annex IV 2(b) account would then look stable.
rubric: Names the Section 7.4 persistence of region disagreement (c4).
Also names the claim that the flips include disagreement about which region is responsible (c2), or the implied instability of the Annex IV 2(b) account.

items.question: Suppose Section 7.6 found that, in the size range covered by the Section 7.4 matched pairs, statements differ more than mechanisms. How would that change the reading of 7.4's persistent region disagreement?
items.answer: In that range, the persistent region disagreement would partly reflect the statement procedure amplifying differences that the mechanisms do not carry, rather than genuinely different mechanisms. It would still undermine the filing, because filed statements remain incompatible. But it would point to the claim map, not the circuits, as the main source.
rubric: Says the region disagreement would partly reflect the procedure amplifying differences, not genuinely different mechanisms.
Says the filing problem would remain because the statements still disagree (the source shifts towards the claim map).

items.question: Does the paper show that sufficiency and comprehensiveness are unreliable metrics for judging circuit faithfulness? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper cites Hsia et al.'s inflation result as one reason to treat the metric as an analytic axis. It does not itself evaluate the quality of any metric, and its protocol deliberately avoids adjudicating which choice is correct.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the paper relies on Hsia et al. as motivation and treats the metric as an axis, without testing metric validity or adjudicating between metrics.

items.question: Does Section 7.4 show that the overseer's account of how concentrated the computation is remains unstable among size-matched circuits? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The 7.4 control removes all size-dependent content from the statement, which includes concentration, and tests only region attribution. It says nothing about the stability of the concentration content.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: size-dependent content such as concentration is removed in that control; only region attribution is tested.

items.question: Does the paper show that integrated edge gradients produces more stable filed statements than the edge attribution patching family? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Discovery objectives are one axis of the grid. The reported finding is only that no single axis, when held fixed, removes the disagreement; the paper does not rank objectives by stability. The comparison is also limited to the library's implementations on one model and one task.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the paper reports that no axis rescues the filing but gives no ranking of discovery objectives by statement stability (and the scope is limited to one model and task).

items.question: Does the paper show that adopting the filability protocol would make filings by different analysts agree? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled; the paper does not claim it. The protocol is disclosure: it makes the specification space and the filer's position within it visible, so disagreement can be examined and challenged. It does not reduce variation, and the paper finds that even standardising an axis does not remove disagreement.
rubric: Answers not settled (or says the paper does not show or claim this).
Reason: the protocol requires disclosure rather than constraining choices, converting an assumed property into an examinable one, and no axis fixing removes disagreement.

items.question: Does the paper show that its claim map is the correct translation of circuits into Annex IV and Article 86 statements? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The claim map is one procedure, fixed in advance and published so it can be attacked and checked. The paper itself says every discretisation between circuit and statement is an analytic choice belonging to the specification space, not a uniquely correct translation.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the map is one fixed, published choice open to attack, and its discretisations are themselves analytic choices rather than a validated correct translation.

items.question: Does the three-quarters claim-flip rate show that about three quarters of pairs of real-world filings by different providers would conflict? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The rate is computed over pairs of specifications in a designed, balanced grid, and any interval is conditional on that grid. Real providers need not choose uniformly from it. The study also covers one model and one task.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Reason: the rate is over all pairs of a designed grid, conditional on the grid, and real filers' choices are not a uniform draw from it (with one model and one task as an added limit).

items.question: Does the paper show that the near-disjoint circuits implement different mechanisms throughout the size range? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Structural difference need not imply functional difference. Section 7.6 finds that over part of the range statements differ more than mechanisms do, which points to functional similarity there, and the relationship varies with size. So the paper does not establish that the mechanisms differ everywhere.
rubric: Answers not settled (and not shown).

Reason: structural difference need not imply functional difference, and over part of the range chance-corrected functional disagreement is smaller than statement disagreement, with the relationship varying by size.
