items.question: Would adding a fifth corruption distribution to the pre-registered GPT-2 grid add exactly 350 discovery cells?
items.answer: Yes. Corruption is nested within the five operators that read it, so the new level crosses 5 operators × 7 objectives × 2 prompt variants × 5 seeds = 350 new cells.
rubric: Answers yes (350 new cells)
Reasons that corruption is nested within only the five corruption-reading operators, giving 5 × 7 objectives × 2 prompt variants × 5 seeds

items.question: Would adding a third prompt variant to the pre-registered GPT-2 grid add exactly 350 discovery cells?
items.answer: No. A prompt variant crosses every objective and every operator–corruption combination. That is 7 × 22 × 5 seeds = 770 new cells, not 350.
rubric: Answers no (it adds 770 cells, not 350)
Reasons that prompt variant is fully crossed with all 7 objectives, the 22 operator–corruption combinations (2 + 5×4) and the 5 seeds

items.question: Would requiring filers to state only the coarsest-granularity statement remove all claim flips between specifications?
items.answer: No. The paper reports that flips include disagreement about which region is responsible even at the coarsest granularity, so coarse-only filing leaves those flips in place.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that flips in region attribution persist at the coarsest granularity

items.question: Would requiring filers to state only the coarsest-granularity statement remove disagreements that arise only in how distributed the computation is?
items.answer: Yes. Granularities are nested, so finer statements refine the coarse region statement by adding distribution and input segment. A disagreement confined to that added detail disappears when only the coarse level is filed.
rubric: Answers yes
Reasons that granularities are nested, so how distributed the computation is belongs only to finer statements, which refine rather than contradict the coarse one

items.question: If two circuits have the same aggregate success rate on IOI, must they agree on which individual examples they succeed on?
items.answer: No. The paper notes that functional agreement in aggregate need not imply agreement on individual examples. Two circuits can be equally accurate while failing on different prompts.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that equal aggregate accuracy is compatible with succeeding and failing on different examples (aggregate agreement need not imply example-level agreement)

items.question: If two circuits succeed and fail on exactly the same IOI examples, must they have the same aggregate success rate?
items.answer: Yes. Identical example-by-example outcomes fix the number of successes, so aggregate accuracy must match. Example-level agreement is the stronger of the two notions.
rubric: Answers yes
Reasons that identical per-example outcomes determine the same success count, so example-level agreement implies aggregate agreement

items.question: If the Pythia-160m replication's overall claim-flip rate differed from GPT-2 small's, could the difference be attributed purely to the change of architecture family?
items.answer: No. The two grids also differ in the seed axis, three levels versus five. The composition of specification pairs, including pairs differing in sampled prompts, is therefore not the same, and the grid change is confounded with the model change.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that the Pythia grid has 3 seed levels rather than 5, so the pair composition differs and confounds the comparison

items.question: If the GPT-2 small grid were first restricted to three seed levels before computing its claim-flip rate, would comparing it with Pythia-160m still be confounded by the number of seed levels?
items.answer: No. Pythia's grid is identical to GPT-2's on every axis except seed count. Restricting GPT-2 to three seeds matches the grid composition, so the seed-count confound is removed. Any remaining difference is conditional on the grids, not a general claim.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that the replication differs from the GPT-2 grid only in seed levels, so matching seed count equalises grid composition

items.question: Two discovered circuits both succeed on every IOI example in the evaluation set. Can Section 7.6's chance-corrected agreement tell whether they implement the same mechanism?
items.answer: No. With perfect accuracy for both circuits, the agreement expected from accuracy alone already equals observed agreement, so kappa is undefined or uninformative. The measurement needs variation in success and failure to separate shared mechanism from shared accuracy.
rubric: Answers no, the measure cannot distinguish them
Reasons that agreement expected from accuracy alone equals the observed agreement when both are always correct, so chance correction leaves nothing to measure (kappa undefined or uninformative)

items.question: Suppose the design used a coarser computational graph without separate query, key and value inputs, so it had far fewer edges but the same components. Would the random-baseline degeneracy described in Section 7.5 begin at the same circuit sizes?
items.answer: No, it would begin at smaller sizes. A size-matched uniform draw covers a larger fraction of a smaller edge set, so it touches every component, and supports only one statement, sooner.
rubric: Answers that degeneracy would set in at smaller circuit sizes
Reasons that with fewer edges a draw of a given size covers a larger fraction of the graph and touches every component earlier

items.question: A standards body evaluates Section 7.3-style 'hold one axis fixed' comparisons by computing each level's claim-flip rate pooled across all circuit sizes. Why might its conclusion about which level stabilises statements be misleading?
items.answer: Fixing a level, for example one metric under the metric-relative threshold rule, can shift the distribution of circuit sizes. A lower pooled within-level flip rate might then reflect size composition rather than stabilisation, so each within-level comparison needs its within-size decomposition.
rubric: States that the comparison can be confounded by circuit size
Reasons that axis levels can change the circuit sizes the threshold rule admits, and size is a hidden channel
Says a within-size decomposition is required

items.question: A filer presents a specification curve showing the share of specifications supporting each region statement, but most specifications under one metric were discarded by the threshold rule. Why might the curve misstate the share of the declared space behind each statement?
items.answer: The curve is built from the surviving pool, whose composition differs from the balanced design. The heavily discarded metric is under-represented, so shares and level–statement associations reflect survivors rather than the declared space. Per-level discard rates are needed to read it.
rubric: States that the shares describe the surviving pool, not the declared space
Reasons that uneven discards across metric levels change composition, so the under-represented level's statements are under-weighted
Mentions per-level discard rates (protocol item 4) as what makes this visible

items.question: A conformity body checks a filing by having a second analyst rerun the exact filed specification and finds an identical circuit and statement. Does this establish filability in the paper's sense?
items.answer: No. Rerunning the same configuration under a pinned environment checks reproducibility, not filability. Filability asks whether a competent analyst working anywhere in the declared space of defensible choices would reach a compatible account, and the paper shows other defensible specifications flip the claim on most pairs.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that filability concerns agreement across the declared space of defensible specifications, not reruns of one configuration (which only test reproducibility)

items.question: Why must the random baseline's edge subsets be matched in size to the discovered circuits, rather than drawn at one fixed size?
items.answer: The statement a subgraph supports depends on its size: how many components it touches and how concentrated it looks under the size categories. Unmatched subsets would therefore differ from discovered circuits for size reasons alone. Matching size isolates whether discovery differs from arbitrary subgraphs.
rubric: States that size itself influences which statements a subgraph can support (components touched, concentration or size categories)
Concludes that unmatched sizes would confound the comparison of discovered and random subgraphs

items.question: The paper says a claim that an explanation is stable is exactly the kind of claim undisclosed flexibility can manufacture. Why, given its results?
items.answer: Defensible specifications flip the claim on about three quarters of pairs. An analyst who tries many configurations could therefore report only those that happen to agree and present the result as stable. Without the declared space and discard rates, a reader cannot see the configurations that disagreed.
rubric: States that an analyst could report only the subset of configurations that agree
Links this to the high flip rate across defensible specifications, and notes the omission is invisible without disclosure of the space

items.question: Why does the phantom specialisation objection threaten the interpretation of the claim-flip result but not the near-disjointness finding of Section 7.1?
items.answer: The objection concedes that circuits are structurally distinct and argues they may still implement the same computation. Near-disjointness is a structural fact the objection leaves intact. What it disputes is whether disagreeing statements reflect real mechanism differences, which is why a functional measurement is needed.
rubric: States that near-disjointness is a structural fact the objection accepts
Reasons that the objection targets whether statement disagreement reflects different mechanisms (it could reflect sampling from an equivalence class)

items.question: Why is the overseer's statement more directly exposed to the threshold axis than a pure region attribution is?
items.answer: The overseer's account includes how concentrated the responsible computation is, which depends on circuit size. Circuit size is set by the threshold rule. Changing the threshold can therefore alter that content even when the region is unchanged.
rubric: States that the overseer's statement includes size-dependent content (how concentrated the computation is)
Reasons that circuit size is an outcome of the threshold rule, so threshold changes feed into that content

items.question: After discards, an analyst proposes reweighting the surviving specifications to restore the design's balanced composition before computing the claim-flip rate. Is that consistent with the paper's approach?
items.answer: No. The paper says the surviving pool's composition is a property of the evidence and should be reported rather than smoothed or adjusted for, with discard rates reported per axis level.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that composition should be reported, not adjusted or smoothed, with per-level discard rates disclosed

items.question: In a filer's sweep, one published discovery objective fails to execute in every cell. Should the filer drop it from the declared specification space or substitute another objective?
items.answer: Neither. Item 1 declares the levels a competent analyst could defend, whether or not they ran. The failing objective stays declared and is reported with a 100% discard rate for that level, without repair or substitution, which also records which configurations ran and which did not.
rubric: Answers that it stays in the declared space and is not substituted or repaired
Reasons that the space lists defensible levels and failures are recorded as discards, reported per axis level

items.question: A regulator proposes mandating one complete configuration on all seven axes for every circuit filing. Is that consistent with the rationale the paper gives for its protocol?
items.answer: No. The protocol is implementable because it does not require the regulator to adjudicate which analytic choice is correct, and full mandating does exactly that. The paper also judges that even fully standardising the metric alone is more than a conformity procedure can reasonably demand.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that mandating a configuration requires adjudicating which choice is correct, which the protocol is designed to avoid (or that even standardising one axis is judged too demanding)

items.question: A reviewer builds a specification curve from a compliant filing and finds the filed region statement is supported by only a small minority of the declared space. What does the paper imply this shows, and what does the protocol require the filer to have supplied?
items.answer: It shows that the opposite statement is defensible by most of the space, which is the situation the paper says filings currently conceal. The reviewer can see this without adjudicating, and item 3 requires the filer to have stated which specification it chose and why.
rubric: States that the filed statement's alternative is defensible across most of the declared space (the filing's position in the space is now visible)
Mentions protocol item 3: stating the chosen specification and why it was selected

items.question: If Section 7.6 had used raw example-level agreement instead of chance-corrected agreement, in which direction would the finding that filings differ more than mechanisms be distorted?
items.answer: It would be exaggerated. Similarly accurate circuits agree on many examples by chance, so raw agreement understates functional disagreement. The regime where statement disagreement exceeds functional disagreement would then appear larger than it is.
rubric: States that the finding would be overstated (the statements-exceed-mechanisms regime would look larger)
Reasons that raw agreement inflates functional agreement through accuracy alone, understating functional disagreement

items.question: Suppose changing the claim map's size-category calibration rule had removed most claim flips. Which result would nonetheless be unaffected, and why?
items.answer: The Section 7.4 result. It removes all size-dependent content from the statement and compares only same-size circuits, so the region attribution it tests does not pass through size categories at all.
rubric: Identifies the Section 7.4 maximum-pressure result (region disagreement among size-matched circuits)
Reasons that 7.4 strips size-dependent content, so size-category calibration does not enter its statements

items.question: If the within-size baseline had shown discovered circuits flipping far less often than random subsets at every size, would that undermine the paper's conclusion that filings are not filable as currently produced?
items.answer: No. The baseline answers whether discovered circuits differ from arbitrary subgraphs, which concerns discovery quality. The filability problem is that defensible specifications produce discovered circuits whose statements flip on about three quarters of pairs, and beating random does not reduce that.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that the baseline tests discovery against arbitrary subgraphs, while filability concerns disagreement among defensible specifications (the three-quarters flip rate stands)

items.question: If Hsia et al. had found that sufficiency and comprehensiveness cannot be inflated, would the paper's case for treating the evaluation metric as an analytic axis collapse?
items.answer: No. Hsia et al. is only one reason. Miller et al. show faithfulness scores are highly sensitive to methodological choices, and the four metrics are published, defensible levels in the library, so the metric remains a consequential choice.
rubric: Answers no
Reasons that the metric axis also rests on Miller et al.'s sensitivity findings and on the metrics being published, defensible levels

items.question: Does the exclusion of optimal ablation make the finding that no analytic axis rescues the filing conservative, in the sense that adding it could only strengthen that finding? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Adding a level widens the space, which bears on overall instability. Whether holding the operator fixed at optimal ablation would remove the disagreement is a within-level comparison the grid never ran.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that optimal ablation was never in the grid, so no within-level comparison at that operator exists (wider space does not determine what fixing at the new level does)

items.question: Does the paper show that holding any two analytic axes fixed together would still leave filed statements in disagreement? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The design holds each axis fixed in turn and compares within its levels. Joint fixing of pairs of axes is not reported, though the paper's caution about standardisation suggests it should not be assumed to help.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that Section 7.3 holds one axis fixed at a time, and joint fixing of two axes is not tested

items.question: Does Section 7.6 show that phantom specialisation holds, meaning structurally distinct circuits implement the same mechanism, over part of the size range? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The result is comparative: over part of the range, statement disagreement exceeds chance-corrected functional disagreement. That does not mean functional disagreement is zero, so it does not establish that the mechanisms are identical.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that the finding is only that statements differ more than mechanisms, which does not imply functional disagreement is absent

items.question: Does the paper show that circuits from different specifications are nearly disjoint at the level of model components (attention heads and MLP blocks), not just edges? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Section 7.1 concerns edge sets in a factorised graph of tens of thousands of edges. Circuits with little edge overlap may still occupy the same region and support the same statement, so component-level overlap is not reported.
rubric: Answers not settled
Reasons that the disjointness result is about edges, and the paper notes edge-disjoint circuits can still support the same region statement, so component overlap is not established

items.question: Would adding a further, finer granularity level to the claim map require running any new discovery cells?
items.answer: No. Granularity is applied by the deterministic claim map to circuits that already exist. It is not one of the factors that multiply to 1,540 discovery cells, so no discovery has to be rerun.
rubric: Asserts that no new discovery cells are needed.
Explains that granularity is applied by the claim map to existing circuits and is not a factor in the 1,540-cell discovery count.

items.question: Would adding an eighth discovery objective to the pre-registered GPT-2 grid require running new discovery cells?
items.answer: Yes. Each objective spans 22 operator–corruption combinations × 2 prompt variants × 5 seeds, which is 220 discovery cells (1,540 / 7). An eighth objective therefore adds 220 cells and 2,640 specifications.
rubric: Asserts that new discovery cells are required.
Gives 220 new cells (1,540/7, or 22 × 2 × 5), optionally 2,640 specifications.

items.question: When a single discovery cell fails to execute, are all the specifications built on that cell lost?
items.answer: Yes. Each cell yields 12 specifications (4 metrics × 3 thresholds, since 18,480 / 1,540 = 12). A failed cell produces no circuit, so all 12 are recorded as discards.
rubric: Asserts that all specifications built on the cell are lost.
States that this is 12 specifications (4 metrics × 3 thresholds).

items.question: When the threshold rule admits no circuit for one metric–threshold combination of a cell that ran successfully, are the other specifications built on that cell also lost?
items.answer: No. Only that one specification is discarded. The cell's other metric–threshold combinations apply their own threshold rule to the same discovery output and can still admit circuits.
rubric: Asserts that the other specifications are not lost.
Explains that metric and threshold are applied per specification on top of the shared discovery output, so the discard is specific to that combination.

items.question: Before any discards, when Section 7.3 holds the evaluation metric fixed, does each metric level contain the same number of specifications?
items.answer: Yes. The metric is fully crossed with everything else, so each of the four levels holds 18,480 / 4 = 4,620 specifications.
rubric: Asserts that the groups are equal.
Gives 4,620 per level, or explains that the metric is fully crossed.

items.question: Before any discards, when Section 7.3 holds the ablation operator fixed, does each operator level contain the same number of specifications?
items.answer: No. Each corruption-reading operator spans four corruption levels, giving 3,360 specifications. Each of the two non-reading operators gives only 840, because corruption is nested.
rubric: Asserts that the groups are unequal.
Attributes this to corruption being nested within the five reading operators: four times as many specifications, about 3,360 versus 840.

items.question: Do two specifications that differ only in threshold share the same discovery cell?
items.answer: Yes. Threshold is one of the 12 metric–threshold combinations applied to each discovery cell. Any statement difference between the two comes from post-discovery selection, not from rerunning discovery.
rubric: Asserts yes.
Explains that threshold (with metric) is applied to a shared discovery output, the 12 specifications per cell.

items.question: Do two specifications that differ only in seed share the same discovery cell?
items.answer: No. Seed is a factor of the 1,540 discovery cells, and it selects different sampled prompts. The two specifications therefore come from separate discovery runs.
rubric: Asserts no.
Explains that seed multiplies the discovery cells (it is part of the cell definition and selects different prompts).

items.question: When Section 7.3 holds the corruption distribution fixed, does every specification in the grid fall into one of its levels?
items.answer: No. Specifications using the two operators that never read the corrupt distribution have no corruption level. That is 140 cells, or 1,680 specifications, which no within-corruption comparison can include.
rubric: Asserts that not every specification falls into a level.
Identifies the specifications using the two non-reading operators (about 1,680 specifications or 140 cells) as the excluded set.

items.question: When Section 7.3 holds the prompt variant fixed, does every specification in the grid fall into one of its levels?
items.answer: Yes. Prompt variant is crossed with every other axis, so each specification uses one of the two variants (9,240 each before discards).
rubric: Asserts yes.
Explains that prompt variant is fully crossed (not nested), so every specification has a level.

items.question: The surviving pool may contain unequal numbers of specifications per evaluation metric. Why must that imbalance come from the threshold rule rather than from cells that failed to execute?
items.answer: A failed cell discards all 12 of its specifications, three under each metric, so cell failures remove specifications equally across metric levels. Uneven survival by metric can only come from specifications for which the metric-relative threshold rule admits no circuit.
rubric: Attributes the metric imbalance to the threshold rule (no-admit discards).
Explains that a cell failure removes all metric levels equally (3 specifications per metric of its 12).

items.question: Why does a claim-flip rate pooled over the full balanced grid weight each corruption-reading ablation operator four times as heavily as each non-reading operator?
items.answer: Corruption is nested within the five reading operators. Each of them appears with four corruption distributions, giving 280 cells, while each non-reading operator appears in only 70 cells. A pooled figure therefore reflects reading operators disproportionately, even though the design is balanced in its nested structure.
rubric: States that reading operators contribute four times as many cells or specifications.
Attributes this to corruption being nested only within the reading operators.

items.question: Bayat Makou et al. already documented phantom specialisation. Why can the paper not simply cite their finding to dismiss the objection for its own grid, rather than measuring functional agreement?
items.answer: Their circuits varied only input statistics with the task held fixed. This grid also varies objectives, operators, metrics and thresholds, so nothing shows that its circuits form one behavioural equivalence class. Whether that holds has to be measured example by example within the grid.
rubric: States that their result cannot be transferred and must be measured within this grid.
Notes that Bayat Makou varied input statistics while this grid varies other axes (operators, metrics, thresholds, objectives).

items.question: Why should an edge-overlap comparison between circuits admitted at different thresholds also be read within size?
items.answer: Overlap expected by chance depends on how large a circuit is relative to the graph. It is near zero at a few hundred edges and grows as circuits approach the graph's size. Pooling overlaps across thresholds mixes different chance levels, which is the same size-channel hazard the paper identifies for the random baseline.
rubric: Asserts that structural comparisons need within-size reading.
Explains that chance overlap rises with circuit size, so pooling mixes different chance baselines.

items.question: Why can a filer give the overseer a coarse statement and the affected person a finer one from the same circuit without the two filed versions contradicting each other?
items.answer: The claim map nests its granularities, so a finer statement refines the coarser one rather than contradicting it. Both are produced by the same deterministic map from the same circuit, so choosing detail by addressee changes how much is said, not what is said.
rubric: Asserts that the two versions cannot contradict each other.
Attributes this to nested granularities (finer refines coarser) applied by one deterministic map to the same circuit.

items.question: Suppose the random baseline drew its edge subsets only from the union of edges that appeared in some discovered circuit. Could it still answer the question the paper's baseline is meant to answer?
items.answer: No. The baseline is meant to show whether discovered circuits behave differently from arbitrary subgraphs of the full edge set. A pool already shaped by discovery is not arbitrary, so the comparison would partly measure discovery against itself.
rubric: Asserts that it could no longer answer the question.
Explains that the baseline must be drawn from the full edge set because a discovery-shaped pool is not arbitrary.

items.question: A provider reruns its filed configuration under all five seeds and gets the same region statement each time. Does this show the filing is filable?
items.answer: No. In this design the seed only changes which prompts are sampled, so it measures evaluation-set variability and is one of seven axes. A competent second analyst could vary the other six, and the paper finds that no single axis governs the disagreement.
rubric: Asserts that seed robustness does not establish filability.
Explains that seed is one axis (evaluation-set variability) and leaves the other axes, where disagreement persists, unexamined.

items.question: Suppose the threshold rule discarded nearly every specification under one evaluation metric, leaving only a handful in that level. Would a bootstrap interval for that metric's within-level claim-flip rate be trustworthy, and what should be reported instead?
items.answer: No. Bootstrap intervals become unreliable when a conditioning group holds only a handful of specifications. That level's quantity should be reported as a point estimate with diagnostics and its discard rate, not repaired with a bespoke estimator.
rubric: Asserts that the interval is not trustworthy.
Recommends a point estimate with diagnostics (and the discard rate) instead of an interval or a bias-corrected estimator.

items.question: A filer's specification curve orders specifications by the statement they support but omits which analytic levels are active for each. What can a reviewer no longer judge?
items.answer: The reviewer cannot tell whether particular analytic levels are associated with particular statements. That is the information needed to judge whether fixing some axis would bring statements together, or whether a filed statement depends on one level choice. Only the share of the space behind each statement remains visible.
rubric: Identifies the lost information as the association between analytic levels and statements.
Links it to judging whether standardising an axis would help, or whether the filed statement depends on a particular level.

items.question: Two analysts each pick a specification from the paper's surviving GPT-2 pool, independently and with every specification equally likely. Roughly how likely are their filed claims to agree, and under what restriction?
items.answer: About one in four, since the claim flips on about three quarters of specification pairs. This holds only conditional on the grid and on uniform selection. Real analysts do not choose uniformly, so the figure says nothing directly about real-world filings.
rubric: Gives about 25% (one quarter) agreement.
Derives it from the three-quarters flip rate.
Notes that it is conditional on the grid and on uniform random choice.

items.question: In a filer's version of the paper's grid, one of the seven discovery objectives fails in every cell and nothing else is discarded. What discard rates would protocol item 4 show for that objective and for each metric level?
items.answer: That objective's level would show 100% discards and the other objectives 0%. Each metric level, like every other axis level, would show about 14.3% (1/7). Only the per-level breakdown locates the loss in one objective.
rubric: States 100% for the failing objective (0% for the others).
States about 14.3% (1/7) for each metric level.
Notes that the per-level report shows where the loss is concentrated.

items.question: A reviewer asks a filer for a p-value testing whether the claim-flip rate differs between two metric levels in its grid. What does the paper imply the filer should provide instead?
items.answer: No p-value, because specifications are a designed grid, not an independent sample. The filer should report the within-level rates, with intervals from resampling specifications (not pairs) read as conditional on the grid. Where groups are small, it should give point estimates with diagnostics.
rubric: Asserts that a p-value is inappropriate.
Explains that specifications are a designed grid, not a sample.
Recommends within-level estimates with specification-resampled, grid-conditional intervals (or point estimates for small groups).

items.question: A filer's statements label computation as 'concentrated' or 'distributed' using a cutoff on the share of heads involved, chosen by its team. The declared specification space lists only the seven discovery axes. What is missing under the paper's principles?
items.answer: The cutoff is a discretisation between circuit and statement, so it is itself an analytic choice. It belongs in the declared space, should come from a committed calibration rule rather than hand selection, and should have its sensitivity reported.
rubric: Asserts that the cutoff must be declared in the specification space.
Explains that every discretisation between circuit and statement is an analytic choice (it should come from a committed calibration rule, with sensitivity reported).

items.question: A team's threshold rule always keeps a fixed number of top-scoring edges. Which of the paper's two pre-registered exclusion types could still occur in their grid?
items.answer: Only cells failing to execute. A fixed-count rule always admits a circuit, so specifications with no admitted circuit cannot arise, and threshold-driven uneven survival across metrics disappears.
rubric: Identifies cell execution failures as the only remaining exclusion type.
Explains that a fixed-count rule always admits a circuit, removing no-admit discards.

items.question: A provider expects that an auditor will check its filing on IOI prompts sampled differently from its own. Which axis of the paper's grid represents that difference, and what does this imply for the filing?
items.answer: The seed axis, because in this design the seed selects which prompts are sampled and so measures evaluation-set variability. The provider should treat prompt sampling as a declared axis and expect statements to possibly differ along it, rather than assuming its sample is neutral.
rubric: Identifies the seed axis (prompt variant is also acceptable if template wording differs).
Explains that seed here selects sampled prompts, so it should be declared in the specification space.

items.question: If Méloux et al. had shown that a behaviour always has a unique explanation under mechanistic interpretability's own criteria, what part of the paper's argument would lose support, and what would not?
items.answer: The premise that defensible variation should yield different circuits, which the paper adopts from them and uses to frame 7.1, would lose its theoretical backing. The measured near-disjointness and claim flips are empirical results of the grid, so they would stand as observations still needing explanation.
rubric: Identifies the non-identifiability premise or expectation behind 7.1 as the part weakened.
States that the empirical findings (disjointness, claim flips) do not depend on it and would remain.

items.question: If Miller et al. had found faithfulness scores insensitive to design choices, would the Section 7.2 claim-flip result lose support?
items.answer: No. Miller et al. motivate treating metric and operator choices as consequential and supply the library. The three-quarters flip rate is measured directly by running the grid through the claim map, so it does not rest on their sensitivity finding.
rubric: Asserts that 7.2 would not lose support.
Explains that the flip rate is measured directly in the grid, while Miller et al. only motivate the axes and supply the instrument.

items.question: Section 7.6 finds a size range where statements differ more than mechanisms. Which protocol item lets a second analyst check whether a given filing's statement procedure is the source of such amplification?
items.answer: Item 2, publishing the claim map as deterministic code. Only with the exact procedure can the analyst map alternative circuits to statements and compare statement disagreement with chance-corrected functional agreement.
rubric: Identifies item 2 (published deterministic claim map).
Explains that amplification is a property of the statement procedure, which must be available to run on alternative circuits.

items.question: If circuits had been nearly disjoint across specifications but their statements had never flipped, which of the paper's conclusions would lose their force?
items.answer: The regulatory conclusions would lose their force: that filings are not filable as produced, that no axis rescues them, and that disagreement survives size control. The paper treats structural variation as a premise, not as the quantity a filing depends on, so disjointness alone would raise no filing problem.
rubric: Identifies the claim-flip and filability conclusions (c2, and with them c3 and c4) as losing force.
Explains that structural difference is only a premise and need not imply statement difference.

items.question: Suppose the Pythia-160m replication found circuits as nearly disjoint as in GPT-2 small, but claim flips far rarer. Which caution in the paper would this illustrate, and which conclusion would look model-specific?
items.answer: It would illustrate the caution that structural difference need not imply statement difference, so edge overlap is not what a filing depends on. The high claim-flip rate would then look specific to GPT-2 small.
rubric: Names the structure-versus-statement caution (c1).
States that the claim-flip result (c2) would look specific to GPT-2 small.

items.question: If edge overlap between circuits perfectly predicted whether their statements agreed, which recommendation in Section 7.3 would lose its rationale?
items.answer: The recommendation that standardisation decisions be made at the level of the statement. Its rationale is that the axes governing structure need not govern statements. If overlap tracked statements, standardising the axis that most changes the edge set would suffice.
rubric: Identifies the recommendation to standardise at the statement level.
Explains that it rests on structure-governing axes possibly differing from statement-governing axes.

items.question: Does the paper give a numerical claim-flip threshold below which a filing counts as filable? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper says filability names a standard rather than a measurement, and its protocol requires disclosure of the specification space, not meeting any numeric cutoff.
rubric: Answers not settled (no threshold is given).
Explains that filability is a standard rather than a measurement and the protocol is disclosure-based.

items.question: Does the paper predict that claim instability will grow in larger models because they have more components? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper notes that larger models enlarge both the space of circuits and the space of statements, and says it is not obvious in which direction the considerations would move. It claims nothing about scale.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that both the circuit and statement spaces grow, so the direction is unclear, and that nothing is claimed about scale.

items.question: Does the paper show that a region attribution stable across specifications would by itself satisfy Annex IV point 2(b)? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. Region attribution is called the core of a 2(b) account and is what Section 7.4 tests. The paper does not argue that it is sufficient, and other obligations (2(e), Article 86) need further content.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Explains that region is described as the core of 2(b), not as sufficient, and that the paper only tests whether it is stable.

items.question: Do discovery cells that fail to execute show that the library's discovery methods are defective? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled, and the paper explicitly disclaims this reading. Failures are recorded as discards that shape the composition of the evidence. The paper says only that robustness of every exported configuration cannot be taken for granted, so filings should record which configurations ran.
rubric: Answers not settled (the paper disclaims the defect reading).
Explains that failures are treated as recorded discards and a reporting matter, not as evidence of defective methods.

items.question: Does the paper show that claim flips affect only the overseer's detailed account, leaving the affected person's coarsest account stable? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Contradicted. The paper states that flips occur even at the coarsest granularity, and that even the coarsest account available to an affected person rests on undisclosed choices.
rubric: Answers contradicted.
Cites the finding that flips occur at the coarsest granularity, including the account available to an affected person.

items.question: Does the paper show that complying with the filability protocol is cheap in absolute terms? Answer supported, contradicted or not settled, and why.
items.answer: Not settled. The paper claims compliance is cheap relative to the sweep that produced the circuit and possible with existing tooling. It gives no absolute cost, which would depend on how expensive the sweep was.
rubric: Answers not settled.
Notes that the cheapness claim is relative to the sweep, not absolute.

rejected.question: Suppose Section 7.6 found that, among size-matched pairs, mechanisms differ more than statements do. How would that bear on reading the Section 7.4 region disagreement as a property of the statement procedure?
rejected.answer: In that regime the statement procedure is coarser than the mechanisms rather than amplifying them. The persistent region disagreement in 7.4 would then reflect real mechanism differences, at least partly, rather than artefacts of the claim map.
rubric: States that the claim map would be coarser than the mechanisms there, not amplifying differences
Concludes that 7.4's region disagreement would then track genuine mechanism differences rather than being produced by the procedure
